1.title: Model Selection, Cost and Token Management
1.text: Welcome to Module eight: Model Selection, Cost and Token Management. This module covers the skills model selection and tradeoffs, cost and token management. Each part of this module comes from the study notes of the same name, so you can read the notes after you watch.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do four things. Opus, Sonnet and Haiku use cases, and the larger model above them. The quality, latency and cost trade-off, and routing. Breaking behavior changes across model releases. Token tracking, cost modeling and the main cost levers: caching, batch, effort, pruning.

1.title: Case Check-In: Tidewater Picks Models
1.text: Our running case is Tidewater Insurance. Tidewater Picks Models. Three jobs: classify every incoming email (millions a month), answer adjuster questions, and investigate complex fraud cases. One model for everything would be either too weak or too expensive.

1.title: Choosing a Model
1.text: Choosing a Model. Haiku (for example Claude Haiku five point five). Strength: Fastest and cheapest. Typical use: High-volume, latency-sensitive work: classification, routing, screening, simple extraction. Sonnet (Claude Sonnet five point five). Strength: Best balance of speed and intelligence. Typical use: Most interactive applications, coding assistants, everyday agents. Opus (Claude Opus five point five). Strength: Strong on long-running agentic and knowledge work. Typical use: Complex coding, multi-step agents, hard analysis; a good default when unsure. Fable (Claude Fable five point one). Strength: Highest capability, slower and costlier. Typical use: The hardest reasoning and long-horizon agentic tasks, when Opus at high effort still falls short.

1.title: Choosing a Model, continued
1.text: Choosing a Model, continued. The figure shows this: Pick the smallest tier that meets the quality bar: Haiku for volume, Sonnet for balance, Opus for long agentic work, Fable for the hardest tasks. Method: define the quality bar with evals (Module sixteen), try the smallest model, move up only when evals fail, and move down when a cheaper model still passes. Route by difficulty (cascade): a cheap model handles the easy bulk; escalate hard or low-confidence cases to a stronger model.

1.title: Choosing a Model, continued
1.text: Choosing a Model, continued. Adaptive thinking support and effort differ by model; check the model page (Module three). "Always the largest model" and "always the smallest model" are both wrong answers: the right model is the cheapest that meets the measured requirement. Current lineup and prices (per million tokens, input or output): Fable five point one ten dollars or fifty dollars Opus five point five four dollars or twenty dollars Sonnet five point five two dollars or ten dollars Haiku five point five from zero dollars and ten cents or zero dollars and fifty cents; all with a one million token context window and up to one hundred twenty-eight thousand output tokens. Model names, tiers and prices change; read the models overview. As of eight November two thousand twenty-six.

1.title: Breaking behavior changes across releases
1.text: Breaking behavior changes across releases. New models can change behavior even with the same prompt, and some parameters are removed or restricted. Examples on current models: manual extended thinking is rejected (use adaptive thinking), sampling parameters are not accepted, and forced tool use is not supported on some models. Therefore: pin the model, read the migration guide before switching, re-run evals on the new model, and roll out gradually. Models are retired on published dates; plan migrations early (Module one). Exam tip: "Upgrade to the newest model" is a release: read the migration notes, re-run evals, adjust prompts and parameters, then deploy. Exam tip: Pick the smallest model that passes your evals; "always the largest" and "always the smallest" are both wrong.

1.title: Know what you spend
1.text: Know what you spend. The figure shows this: Cost per request: input, output (including thinking), and cache tokens at their own prices; batch halves the price. Track usage from the usage field of every response (input, output, cache creation and cache read tokens) and aggregate by feature, user and model. Output tokens cost more than input tokens, and thinking tokens are output tokens.

1.title: Know what you spend, continued
1.text: Know what you spend, continued. Estimate before sending with the token counting endpoint (an estimate) to budget, route and set limits. Cost modeling: estimate tokens per request times requests per month times price, for each model; add caching and batch effects; compare options before building. Example (illustrative): one million requests a month, eight hundred input and one hundred fifty output tokens each, on a model priced two dollars input and ten dollars output per million: input eight hundred million tokens equals one thousand six hundred dollars output one hundred fifty million tokens equals one thousand five hundred dollars total about three thousand one hundred dollars a month; with a cached six hundred-token prefix read at a fraction of the input price the input cost falls sharply.

1.title: The cost levers
1.text: The cost levers. Smaller model or routing. Effect: Lower price and latency. Watch out for: Quality: prove with evals. Prompt caching. Effect: Cache reads cost a fraction of input; faster. Watch out for: Only stable prefixes; minimum length; T T L. Cache check-pointing (breakpoints). Effect: Cache the growing conversation prefix at chosen points. Watch out for: Up to four breakpoints; order matters. Batch A P I (application programming interface). Effect: fifty percent lower price. Watch out for: Up to twenty-four h; not for waiting users. Lower effort. Effect: Fewer thinking and output tokens. Watch out for: Capability loss on hard tasks. Prune context. Effect: Fewer input tokens: trim tool output, compact, drop stale history. Watch out for: Do not drop needed facts.

1.title: The cost levers, continued
1.text: The cost levers, continued. Limit output. Effect: Concise instructions, sensible max tokens, structured output. Watch out for: Truncation if too low.

1.title: The cost levers, continued
1.text: The cost levers, continued. The figure shows this: Cost levers and their trade-offs: every saving needs a check that quality still passes the evals. Exam tip: Reduce cost without breaking quality: pick the lever that matches the workload (cache repeated prefixes, batch the non-urgent work, route easy cases to a small model) and verify with evals.

1.title: Module Recap
1.text: Here is the recap. Tiers: Haiku fastest and cheapest (volume), Sonnet balance, Opus long agentic work (good default), Fable hardest tasks. Method: Evals set the bar; smallest model that passes; step up only when evals fail. Routing: Cheap model for the bulk, escalate hard cases. Releases: Pin the model; read migration notes; re-run evals; params can change. Track: usage fields; token counting endpoint (estimate). Cost: Output greater than input price; thinking equals output; cache write about one point two five times, read about zero point one times; batch −fifty percent. Levers: Smaller model, caching and breakpoints, batch, lower effort, prune context, limit output.

1.title: Practice Question 1
1.text: Question one. Tidewater must label millions of incoming emails quickly and cheaply with a simple category set. Which model choice fits? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C. High-volume, simple, latency-sensitive tasks fit the fastest, cheapest tier once evals show the quality is sufficient.

1.title: Practice Question 2
1.text: Question two. A team always uses the largest model and the bill is high. Evals show a mid-tier model passes. What should they do? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D. Choose the cheapest model that meets the measured requirement.

1.title: Practice Question 3
1.text: Question three. A system uses a cheap model for most requests and a stronger model only when confidence is low. What is this pattern? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D. Routing sends easy cases to a small model and escalates hard ones.

1.title: Practice Question 4
1.text: Question four. A developer upgrades the model name in production and answers change unexpectedly, and a parameter now returns an error. What should have been done? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B. Model changes can alter behavior and remove parameters; treat them as releases.

1.title: Practice Question 5
1.text: Question five. Where can a developer see how many tokens a request actually used? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A. The response usage reports input, output and cache tokens for tracking.

1.title: Practice Question 6
1.text: Question six. A developer wants to estimate the input size of a large prompt before sending it. What helps? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A. Token counting estimates input tokens so you can budget and route.

1.title: Practice Question 7
1.text: Question seven. Output tokens are priced higher than input tokens. Which change is the most direct way to reduce output cost? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A. Shorter, structured output lowers the more expensive tokens.

1.title: Practice Question 8
1.text: Question eight. An application resends the same twenty thousand-token policy text in every request. Which lever reduces its cost most? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B. Cache reads of a repeated prefix cost a fraction of normal input and are faster.

1.title: Practice Question 9
1.text: Question nine. Select two. Which two describe good model selection practice? The five options are on the screen. The answers are C and E. Evals define "good enough" and must be repeated on each model change.

1.title: Practice Question 10
1.text: Question ten. Select two. Which two levers reduce cost for the nightly bulk re-tagging of old claims? The five options are on the screen. The answers are C and D. Non-urgent bulk work suits batch pricing and routing to a cheaper model.

1.title: Answers at a Glance
1.text: Here are all ten answers. Question one: C. Question two: D. Question three: D. Question four: B. Question five: A. Question six: A. Question seven: A. Question eight: B. Question nine: C and E. Question ten: C and D. In the next module, we continue the course.
